pages.name: Steel and wood
pages.text: Heat moves from hotter to colder by itself. A steel rail and a wooden rail sit in a 20 °C room. Both thermometers read 20 °C. A warm hand rests on each. Heat runs out of each hand into its rail. It runs much faster into the steel, because metal passes heat far more easily than wood. So the steel feels colder. Nothing called cold flows into your hand. You feel how fast heat leaves your skin.

pages.name: Which is colder?
pages.task: Both rails spent the night in the same 20 °C room. Which one is colder?
pages.why: A night in one room brings everything to the room's temperature. So both rails are at 20 °C. The steel only feels colder. Heat leaves your hand faster into the metal, and that is what your skin feels.

pages.name: Heat made in the copper
pages.text: Now a loaded cable, cut across. A copper core sits inside a ring of insulation, with the room's air around it. Current through the copper makes heat, its [[I²R losses]]. This cable has 8 mΩ in each metre. At 50 A that is 0.008 × 50² = 20 W in each metre. All that heat has to get out, through the insulation and into the air. Half the current makes a quarter of the losses.

pages.name: What happens next?
pages.task: The current switches on at 50 A. The copper starts at the room's 30 °C. What does it do next?
pages.why: At first no heat leaves, so all 20 W warms the copper. As it warms, the gap to the room grows, and more heat flows out. So the warming slows. When the heat leaving matches the 20 W made, it stops rising. Here that is at 70 °C.

pages.name: Switch on
pages.text: The current switches on at 50 A. The copper warms until the heat leaving matches the losses. Heat [[conducts]] through the copper and its insulation. From the surface, the air carries it off by [[convection]]. [[Radiation]] carries some as infrared, which needs no air. Each layer has a [[thermal resistance]]: its degrees of rise for each watt leaving each metre. Insulation 0.5 and still air 1.5 make 2 K·m/W. So the copper rises 20 × 2 = 40 °C, to 70 °C. The insulation takes 10 °C of that drop, and the air 30 °C. Once the current is off, the copper cools back to the room along the same kind of curve.

pages.name: With the extra wrap
pages.task: Now add the extra wrap. Its thermal resistance is 2 K·m/W. It is still 50 A in a 30 °C room. Where does the copper settle?
pages.why: The way out is now 0.5 + 2 + 1.5 = 4 K·m/W. So the rise is 20 × 4 = 80 °C. Add the room's 30 °C, and the copper settles at 110 °C. That is well over the 70 °C limit. The wrap alone takes 40 °C of the drop.
pages.alt: A cable cut across: a copper core, its insulation, an extra wrap and the room's air. Below, the copper's temperature after switch-on, 100 minutes in: 109 °C.

pages.name: How long it takes
pages.text: It climbs like a capacitor charging through a resistor. Each metre of this cable needs 300 J to warm by 1 °C. That is its [[heat capacity]], its mc. Thermal resistance × heat capacity gives the [[time constant]], τ, just as RC does. Here that is 2 × 300 = 600 s, or 10 minutes. After one τ the copper has made 63% of its rise, so it is near 55 °C. By about five, 50 minutes, it has all but settled.

pages.name: Twice the heat capacity
pages.task: Another cable needs 600 J to warm each metre by 1 °C. Its losses and thermal resistances are the same. What happens after switch-on?
pages.answer: It settles at 70 °C, taking twice as long
pages.why: The rise is still 20 × 2 = 40 °C, so it settles at 70 °C. Heat capacity only sets the time. τ is now 2 × 600 = 1,200 s, or 20 minutes, twice as long.

pages.name: Carrying less
pages.text: To keep to 70 °C, carry less current. With the extra wrap, each watt lifts the copper twice as far, so the losses must halve. Losses go with current squared, so the current falls to 0.707 × 50 A, about 35 A. That is the reason behind Ci. A fan works the other way. At 50 A it holds the copper at 50 °C. A fan lowers the air's thermal resistance, so the copper settles cooler. Each degree warmer in the room makes the copper a degree hotter.

pages.name: A hot room
pages.task: No wrap now, and the room is at 40 °C. 50 A makes 20 W in each metre. What is the most current that keeps the copper at 70 °C?
pages.why: The headroom is 70 − 40 = 30 °C. That allows 30 ÷ 2 = 15 W in each metre. Losses go with current squared, so the current is 50 × √(15 ÷ 20). That is 50 × 0.866, about 43 A. The factor is also √(30 ÷ 40), the new headroom over the old. It depends only on the temperatures. So it holds for any cable rated in a 30 °C room with a 70 °C limit. That is where Ca comes from.

pages.name: A motor and a heat sink
pages.text: The same sum works for any part that makes heat. A motor's winding makes it. It leaves through the insulation, the iron and the frame into the air. A fan on the shaft eases that last step. A motor's time constant is from half an hour to five hours. Stopped, its fan stops too. The way out gets harder, so it cools more slowly. A protection relay runs this same curve to judge the winding's heat. A transistor's heat leaves through its case and a finned heat sink.

pages.name: A transistor
pages.task: A transistor's losses are 10 W. Its way out to the air through a heat sink is 3 °C per W. That is for the whole part, not each metre. The room is at 25 °C. How hot does it run?
pages.why: The rise is losses × thermal resistance: 10 × 3 = 30 °C. Add the room's 25 °C. So it runs at 55 °C.

pages.name: Just after switch-on
pages.task: A cable's losses are 20 W in each metre. Each metre needs 300 J to warm by 1 °C. How fast does it warm just after switch-on?
pages.why: At switch-on no heat leaves yet, so all 20 W goes into warming. Each °C takes 300 J. So it warms 20 ÷ 300 = 0.067 °C each second. That is about 4 °C a minute.
